=========
Stability
=========

Perhaps the trickiest part of finite element modeling is making sure a model is stable. That may
sound trivial, but in finite element analysis it is nuanced. If you are getting "singularity"
errors in your model, it may not be as stable as you think it is. Remember that just because a
model is static does not mean it is stable.

Degrees of Freedom
==================
In 3 dimensions there are 6 "degrees of freedom" for motion to occur in. An object can translate
in either the X, Y or Z direction, and it can rotate about the X, Y or Z axis. These 3 translations
and 3 rotations together sum to 6 degrees of freedom. For an object to be stable, all 6 degrees
of freedom need to be stabilized

Rigid body motion occurs when the entire structure can move as a unit in one of the 6 degrees of
freedom. This occurs when there is insufficient support for the structure. When rigid body motion
occurs, the stiffness matrix is "singular", and unsolvable. Adding supports can eliminate this type

## Summary

The historical workflow silently returned huge, solver-dependent garbage (≈1e17, sparse ≠ dense) for `frame_b` while reporting it as a finite, completed result.

**Root cause** — `frame_b` is a multi-DOF bending mechanism: its free-free stiffness submatrix `K11` is rank-deficient (rank 13/14, condition 8.6e16), but *no single diagonal is zero* (min |diag| ≈ 18.6). `_check_stability` only scanned for exactly-zero diagonals on free DOFs, so it passed; the near-singular solve then returned finite-but-meaningless values that differed between the sparse and dense solvers. The manual (`paper.md` / `docs/source/stability.rst`) states both rigid-body motion and nodal/mechanism instabilities "appear as a singular, unsolvable stiffness system" and that `check_stability=True` isolates them.

**Fix** — `source/Pynite/Analysis.py:109` (`_check_stability`): kept the existing per-DOF diagonal scan (clear single-DOF messages) and added a rank/singularity test on the free-DOF submatrix `K11`:
- Dense / small sparse matrices → exact `numpy.linalg.matrix_rank` (gold-standard SVD; tolerance matches numpy's `~1/(n·eps)`).
- Large sparse matrices → condition estimate via `scipy.sparse.linalg.svds` extreme singular values, so large models aren't densified; on estimation failure it defers to the diagonal scan + solver-time exception rather than risk a false positive.

This is gated by the documented `check_stability` option (the workbench already passes `True`), flows through every analysis path (`analyze`, `analyze_linear`, `analyze_PDelta`, `analyze_modal`), and is general — not fixture-specific. The public workbench is untouched.

- `frame_a` (supported): 4/4 paths `completed`, finite, sparse/dense consistent (max disp ≈ 0.4366) — unchanged from before.
